title: Black Monday Fears Grip Wall Street as Traders Lose $52 Million on AI Stock Bets
detail:
Black Monday Fears Grip Wall Street as Traders Lose $52 Million on AI Stock Bets
Lockridge Okoth
Sun, October 18, 2026 at 10:51 AM MST 3 min read
^GSPC
^IXIC

CNN's Fear & Greed Index sank to 18 on Friday, deep in "Extreme Fear," after the Nasdaq fell 4.5% for the week. The reading lands one day before Black Monday turns 39, and crash calls are spreading online.

Traders lost nearly $52 million on leveraged AI and chip stock bets in 10 minutes on Saturday, with Wall Street shut.

Why Are AI Stocks Dragging Wall Street Into Extreme Fear?

The gauge scores investor mood from 0 to 100 using seven market signals, each measured against its own recent history, and all seven count equally. The seven are:

Market momentum: whether the S&P 500 is trading above or below its average over the past 125 trading days.

Stock price strength: how many New York Stock Exchange stocks are hitting 52-week highs compared with 52-week lows.

Stock price breadth: how much trading volume is going into rising stocks compared with falling ones, measured by the McClellan Volume Summation Index.

Put and call options: how many bets on falling prices (puts) traders are buying compared with bets on rising prices (calls), as a five-day average.

Market volatility: the VIX, Wall Street's "fear index," compared with its 50-day average.

Safe-haven demand: how stocks have performed against Treasury bonds over the past 20 trading days.

Junk bond demand: the extra yield investors want for holding riskier company bonds instead of safer, investment-grade ones.

Real-time stock market Fear & Greed Index. Source: Feargreedtracker.com

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 11.4% for the week, its worst run since April 2025, according to Investing.com. The Dow still rose 0.7%.

CoreWeave, a cloud firm renting out AI computing power, fell about 25%. Its bonds hit new lows amid a broader AI debt glut.

Hot inflation data also revived bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike, which would raise borrowing costs.

"Hot inflation data suggests interest rates will remain higher for longer," Michael O'Rourke of Jones Trading stated.

Information technology makes up roughly 39% of the S&P 500, according to CME. Index-fund holders are heavily exposed.

Could Black Monday Happen Again Without Brakes?

On October 19, 1987, the Dow lost 22.6% in one day, per the Federal Reserve. No trading brakes existed then.

Today, a 7% or 13% S&P 500 drop pauses trading for 15 minutes. A 20% fall shuts markets for the day.

Those brakes skip perpetual futures, crypto-exchange contracts tracking stock prices around the clock. When prices fall, exchanges force-close borrowed bets, and each forced sale can push prices lower.

Roughly $38 million of Saturday's losses hit traders betting on higher prices.

title: Wall Street veteran cuts S&P 500 target but keeps huge bet
detail:
Wall Street veteran cuts S&P 500 target but keeps huge bet
Faizan Farooque, Aparajita Chatterjee
Sun, October 18, 2026 at 10:07 AM MST 5 min read
^GSPC

Although Ed Yardeni has become increasingly wary of the stock market, he hasn't given up on one of Wall Street's most ambitious long-term projections.

Yardeni Research now expects the S&P 500 to finish 2026 at 7,900, after moving its previous 8,400 year-end target to mid-2027. The reason is not deteriorating corporate profits. It is how much investors may be willing to pay for them.

The firm lowered its year-end forecast for the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio to 18.6 from 19.8, according to an Oct. 14 note from Yardeni Research. Yardeni still expects earnings of $425 per share in 2027 and no U.S. recession through the end of the decade.

Investors face a strange situation. Yardeni still expects the S&P 500 to reach 10,000 by the end of the decade, but valuations may continue to fall even as earnings rise.

That difference is important for anyone with a 401(k) or an S&P 500 index fund. In essence, Yardeni argues that the bull market may endure even without stock prices rising steadily.

Companies may only need to earn their way up to the next step.

Yardeni says the S&P 500 has a valuation problem

Following the market's drop on October 14, Yardeni's warning gained additional attention.

The S&P 500 dropped 1.1% to 7,718.94 that session, while the Nasdaq Composite and Russell 2000 each fell 1.9%. Semiconductor stocks fell even harder, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF dropping 4.5%, according to Yardeni Research.

These losses align with the danger that Yardeni has been pointing out since September: profits may remain robust while investors decide they are no longer prepared to assign ever-higher values to them.

Because there are two fundamental engines driving stock prices, the distinction is significant. Businesses may increase profits, or investors may consent to pay a larger multiple for those profits.

Yardeni believes the first engine is still operational.

The second seems to be less trustworthy.

"Our concern isn't earnings; it's stock valuations," said Ed Yardeni.

Yardeni Research has maintained its 2027 S&P 500 earnings estimate at $425 per share, only slightly above the analyst consensus of $423.08 cited by the firm on Oct. 14.

Yardeni has already raised the likelihood of a pessimistic conclusion to 30% and decreased the subjective probability of its positive "Roaring 2020s" scenario from 80% to 70%.

The firm cited greater geopolitical and market risks while continuing to expect the U.S. economy to avoid a recession through the end of the decade.

All he's done is increase the bar for stocks.

title: Should You Invest in the S&P 500 Right Now or Wait? There's 1 Clear Answer

Should You Invest in the S&P 500 Right Now or Wait? There's 1 Clear Answer
Leo Sun, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 18, 2026 at 9:50 AM MST 4 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has generated an average annual total return of about 10% since its inception in 1957. However, the index has also gone through some wild swings over the past seven decades -- and those downturns shook out many long-term investors.

Over the past 12 months, the S&P 500 has risen 15% and trades just 2% below its all-time high. It also trades at 21 times forward earnings, compared to its average forward multiple of 17 for the past 25 years. Those numbers suggest it might not be the best time to invest in the S&P 500 via an exchange-traded fund (ETF) such as Vanguard's S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

However, the S&P 500 has also consistently rewarded investors who simply tuned out the near-term noise, stayed invested through downturns, and focused on the long-term gains. So should you invest in the S&P 500 today, even though it looks historically expensive?

Why is the S&P 500 such a resilient investment?

The S&P 500 includes the 500 largest companies in the United States. To join that elite club, they must have a market cap of at least $22.7 billion, have been profitable for at least the past four quarters, and have adequate liquidity and trading volume.

A company can't join the index until 12 months after its IPO, and at least 10% of its shares must be publicly traded. It also excludes certain companies -- including master limited partnerships (MLPs), business development companies (BDCs), and closed-end funds (CEFs) -- which don't issue common stock.

The S&P 500 rebalances itself quarterly to add rising stars and prune its laggards, and adjusts their weights based on their market caps. Over the long term, most actively managed funds struggle to outperform the S&P 500's automated indexing strategy.

That's why Vanguard's founder, John Bogle, advised investors to simply "buy the haystack" instead of searching for individual needles. Today, the S&P 500's biggest components include Nvidia (8.4% of the index), Apple (7.4%), Microsoft (5.8%), Amazon (3.7%), and Alphabet (3.1%). That makes it an easy way to gain instant exposure to the country's top companies without having to do too much homework on each stock.

But is there a "right" time to invest in the S&P 500?

The S&P 500 is a balanced investment for long-term investors, but they must be able to withstand double-digit drawdowns without panicking. Over the past two decades, the S&P 500 experienced peak-to-trough declines of 57% from Oct. 2007 to March 2009, 34% from Feb. to March 2020, and 25% from Jan. 2022 to Oct. 2022.

Mike McGlone said Bitcoin was "rolling over from an extended plateau akin to 2018 and 2022."

He said that "dominoes could tumble" if it failed to prove strength.

Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer said "a new 4-year cycle bull market could be underway" for Bitcoin, adding that "bull markets rarely start with" a narrative.

Mike McGlone, a Bloomberg Intelligence senior commodity strategist, said on Sunday that Bitcoin (BTC) "may have to prove strength, because if it doesn't, dominoes could tumble" for stocks and metals, even as Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer said a new bull market for crypto could already be underway.

McGlone explained that Bitcoin was "rolling over from an extended plateau akin to 2018 and 2022," based on a chart of 50-week moving averages. He described Bitcoin as "a leading indicator for risk assets since its inception in 2009."

Source: @mikemcglone11/x

According to him, the S&P 500 (SPX), the Bloomberg Commodity All Metals Total Return Subindex and copper have not followed Bitcoin lower, as they did in earlier crypto bear markets, which set the period apart. "Is the first-born crypto issuing a warning or a feint?" he wrote.

McGlone also called October "notorious for market inflection points" and said that Federal Reserve rate-hike expectations "may signal an endgame for rapidly rising risk-assets, wealth creation and inflation."

So far, the month has not gone Bitcoin's way. The apex cryptocurrency is down more than 2% in October and on track for its first back-to-back losing October in more than a decade.

Bull Markets Rarely Start With A Narrative
Source: @TimmerFidelity/x

Timmer, Fidelity's director of global macro, read Bitcoin's chart differently, saying that "a new 4-year cycle bull market could be underway," based on Bitcoin's power law patterns. "There doesn't seem to be a narrative, but then again, bull markets rarely start with one," Timmer said. His chart placed Bitcoin's current reading in the area Fidelity labeled the "accumulation zone."

Liquidity Holds The Key

Both strategists flagged tighter conditions in the near term. Timmer said gold and Bitcoin "both remain in holding patterns," and added that gold saw steady inflows but continued "to be held down by a deceleration in global liquidity growth," which he tied to tightening financial conditions.

The Fed raised its target range to 3.75% to 4.00% in September and is scheduled to meet again between October 27 and October 28.

Bitcoin's price fell 0.2% over the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around BTC moved to the 'extremely bearish' from 'bearish' zone, while chatter around it stayed at 'low' levels over the past day.

Cathie Wood, chief of Ark Investment Management, often buys tech stocks during selloffs, betting on their long-term growth potential.

That's what she just did with CoreWeave (CRWV), buying about $11.8 million worth of shares as the AI cloud computing company's stock plunged amid growing concerns over its debt.

Last year, her flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. So far this year, Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is up 6.15% as of writing, while the S&P 500 has surged 11.89%, Yahoo Finance data shows.

Wood gained a reputation after Ark Innovation ETF delivered a rosy 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the ETF tumbled more than 60%.

Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of Oct. 16, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -6.59%, while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 11.37% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar.

Cathie Wood remains optimistic about AI and tech revolution

Wood focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, but their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds.

Over the decade ended 2025, Ark Innovation ETF's losses wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to a report by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott. That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking. 

Wood defended her investment strategy after an audience member at a recent summit questioned ARK's performance compared with Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ).

Related: Cathie Wood buys $17.3 million of surging AI stock

"I welcome the question. Investors deserve to understand both their returns and the decisions behind them," Wood said in a post on X on Oct. 5.

She argued that ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and QQQ are built differently. QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, while ARK actively invests in companies it believes are driving disruptive innovation across industries including health care, financial services and transportation.

Wood has long been optimistic about AI, which she sees as a major driver of productivity, economic growth, and corporate profits in the years ahead. She has also pushed back against recent fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

On Sept. 12, Wood reposted a post by David Sacks on X, saying he makes a good case that the "AI will kill humanity" headlines were deliberately orchestrated and were thus unreliable.

According to S&P Global's Global Market Intelligence, more than 80% of the companies in the S&P 500 index pay a dividend. Because the opportunity set is large, income-focused investing is a popular strategy among the retail crowd.

It makes sense why. Investing in growth stocks means betting on future earnings that may or may not materialize. Value investing, on the other hand, relies on the market eventually agreeing with your assessment of a particular bargain opportunity. There is uncertainty with these strategies.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Dividends provide a cash inflow to investors in up and down markets. And if you reinvest these distributions, it can boost the total return.

But it's important to understand that not all dividends are created equal. It all depends on the business that's backing them. Two consumer stocks help explain this line of thinking.

Coca-Cola (NYSE: KO) shares pay a dividend yield of 2.3%. Nike (NYSE: NKE) stock pays a dividend yield of 4.4%. Here's why only one of these dividend stocks is a better buy in October.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Both companies have remarkable dividend streaks

It's a good idea to first establish why these companies are elite at returning capital to shareholders. They both have incredible dividend streaks going right now.

Coca-Cola has raised its dividend for 64 consecutive years. That makes it a Dividend King, a business with at least 50 straight years of dividend increases.

That streak says nothing of the magnitude of the hikes. In the past decade, the beverage stock's dividend has grown by 51%.

Nike has raised its dividend for 24 straight years. That's a shorter streak than Coca-Cola's, but still an impressive one. If history is any indication, the sportswear company will raise the payout later this year.

Nike's dividend growth has been better than Coca-Cola's. The former's payouts have risen by 128% over the last 10 years.

It depends on what you care about most

When choosing which of these two stocks is the better buy in October, investors need to take some critical information into account. It comes down to business quality.

Both Coca-Cola and Nike possess wide economic moats. The soft drink giant has one of the strongest brands on Earth that drives customer loyalty and pricing power. The sportswear leader, which has admittedly struggled in recent years, has also been a globally recognized brand for decades.

title: The 10-Year Treasury Is Above 5% for the First Time in Almost 20 Years. History Says This Is How the S&P 500 Index Will Perform Over the Next 12 Months.
detail:
The 10-Year Treasury Is Above 5% for the First Time in Almost 20 Years. History Says This Is How the S&P 500 Index Will Perform Over the Next 12 Months.
Neil Patel, The Motley Fool

^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

On the morning of Thursday, Oct. 15, the 10-year Treasury yield sat at 5.06%. It has been making headlines ever since it crossed 5% about three weeks ago. This is viewed by experts as being the most important number in global finance. That's because it sets the risk-free rate of return that anchors pricing, mortgages, corporate borrowing costs, and valuations across the entire economy.

Besides passing this threshold in late September, the 10-year Treasury yield last closed above 5% on July 19, 2007. Almost 20 years have passed since investors have seen it at this level. When rare events like this occur, it might be time to pay attention to what's going on.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Markets are extremely complex and interconnected, and the current situation might affect your portfolio. Investors naturally want to know what comes next for the stock market, and history says this is how the S&P 500 index could perform in the coming 12 months.

Image source: Getty Images.
Drawing parallels to a different era

Over the 12 months following July 19, 2007, the popular stock market benchmark fell 19%. And over the subsequent five years, it was down 11%. This might draw a pessimistic outlook from investors.

In the four years leading up to it closing above 5% on that date in July 2007, the 10-year Treasury saw its yield rise 26%. This was supported by the Federal Reserve aggressively hiking the fed funds rate. The U.S. economy was registering strong growth, and one of the goals was to get ahead of above-average inflation.

That backdrop mimics what we see today. Just in the past 12 months, the 10-year Treasury yield has soared 26%. The central bank has started to raise rates due to stubborn inflation. And as was the case in July 2007, the S&P 500 is currently in all-time record territory and in the middle of a multiyear bull run.

After looking at the parallels, investors might have a gloomy view.

Why this time could be different

However, there are some important differences that shouldn't be ignored. After 2007, stocks performed poorly because of the onset of the Great Financial Crisis. Banks loaded up on risky subprime mortgages, packaging them into complex securities that were sold to third-party investors to raise capital to lend even more. This contributed to the real estate bubble popping, which rippled through the financial system.

title: Jeffrey Gundlach sees a hidden danger beneath the S&P 500
detail:
Jeffrey Gundlach sees a hidden danger beneath the S&P 500
Faizan Farooque, Robert Davey
Sun, October 18, 2026 at 6:33 AM MST 6 min read
^GSPC

Jeffrey Gundlach thinks the stock market looks much healthier than it really is.

Despite seeing the S&P 500 stay close to record highs, the CEO and chief investment officer of DoubleLine Capital likened the market to a "hollow tree," with weakness lurking beneath those peak highs.

His evidence is striking. MarketWatch calculated that 80% of S&P 500 companies were at least 10% below their 52-week highs at the start of October, while 39% had fallen at least 20%. In other words, much of the index was already experiencing correction- or bear-market-sized declines even though the benchmark itself remained close to a record.

Even for investors who never choose particular equities, that is important. Due to the S&P 500 fund's weighting toward the largest firms in the market, a few massive technology corporations may maintain the index's strength while hundreds of smaller participants suffer.

And Gundlach's warning has gained relevance since he made it. More than four in ten S&P 500 stocks were down for 2026 as of Oct. 12, while stress has started appearing in the debt financing the artificial intelligence boom, TheStreet reported.

The S&P 500's ability to continue climbing is no longer the only issue.

It is the amount of weakness the index can conceal before investors become aware of it.

Gundlach says the S&P 500 is weaker than it looks

Gundlach used a real tree as the inspiration for his metaphor.

During an interview with Rosenberg Research founder David Rosenberg, Gundlach described a roughly 100-year-old silver maple at his Buffalo, N.Y., home. The tree had appeared healthy until a large limb suddenly broke away. Only afterward did it become clear how badly the tree had deteriorated internally.

Because the S&P 500 is based on market capitalization, it may stay close to a record. Gains from the biggest firms have a much bigger impact on the index than decreases from smaller members.

Such conditions may lead to a discrepancy between what is happening to the average stock and the index that investors see on television.

"You've got to wait for the branch to fall off," said Gundlach.

A Reuters analysis published Oct. 12 seems to support Gundlach's view of underlying weakness in the stock market. It found that the S&P 500 was up roughly 14% in 2026, even though more than 200 of its members were down for the year. A quarter of the index had fallen at least 11%, while the median S&P 500 stock was up only about 4%.

When investors discuss poor market breadth, they are referring to the fact that fewer equities are taking part in the headline gain.

If you own an S&P 500 index fund, you own a slice of Meta Platforms. That means the company's next earnings report lands in your retirement account whether you follow the stock or not.

This one comes with an unusual line item. It's a bill for how Facebook and Instagram treated teenagers.

Meta Platforms (META) will release third-quarter results after the market closes on Oct. 21, the company said in a release. The company brought in about $201 billion in revenue in 2025, the Associated Press reported, which makes it one of the biggest earners inside the funds millions of Americans hold for retirement.

Wall Street has been warming to its artificial intelligence push. "Introducing Muse, the personal agent that understands your goals and works 24/7 to get things done for you," said CEO Mark Zuckerberg when Meta launched the Muse agent on Sept. 8.

However, the bill for Meta's past is arriving at the same moment as the bill for its future. Both will show up in the numbers you see on Oct. 21.

According to a Bank of America research report dated Oct. 16 and reviewed by TheStreet, Meta's third-quarter profit is likely to look far weaker than Wall Street expects, even as its ad business keeps growing at a healthy clip.

What Bank of America expects on Oct. 21

BofA expects revenue of $63.8 billion, ahead of the $63.3 billion consensus and near the top of Meta's own guidance range of $61 billion to $64 billion. That would mean roughly 25% growth from a year earlier.

Profit is a different story. BofA cut its third-quarter earnings estimate to $3.79 a share from $7.08, below the Street's $6.08, because it expects Meta to book a one-time $10 billion legal charge in the quarter.

Here's what that means in plain terms. Earnings that would have come in near $7 for every share you own, now land closer to $4 for the quarter, almost entirely because of one legal bill.

The BofA research note points to several other numbers worth watching:

Instagram's global daily users rose six percent from a year earlier in the third quarter, while Facebook's fell eight percent, according to Sensor Tower data.

U.S. users spent an average of 58 minutes a day on Instagram in September, up 12%, versus 34 minutes on Facebook, down ten percent.

Muse passed 8.9 million downloads and 2.23 million daily active users, as of Oct. 12.

BofA expects Meta to guide fourth-quarter revenue to between $71.5 billion and $74.5 billion, up 19% to 24% from a year earlier.

HSBC expects third-quarter corporate earnings to provide further support for global equity markets, citing improving profit forecasts, growing demand for artificial intelligence computing capacity and signs of increased AI monetisation.

In a research note published on Tuesday, Alastair Pinder, the bank's head of emerging market and global equity strategy, maintained a positive outlook on equities despite rising bond yields and pressure on stock valuations.

The bank identified corporate earnings announcements and developments in AI-related revenue generation as potential factors influencing market performance during the reporting season.

S&P 500 Valuations Decline as Bond Yields Rise

Global equities have remained relatively stable despite recent selling in bond markets, with the S&P 500 approaching record levels.

However, HSBC noted that higher Treasury yields have affected equity valuations.

According to the bank, the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio has declined 16.5% since late 2025. Additionally, 27% of companies in the index have experienced valuation multiple reductions exceeding 20% this year.

HSBC estimates that each additional 50-basis-point increase in the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note would reduce the S&P 500's forward earnings multiple by a further 4.3%.

The bank also identified differences between headline market volatility measures and the implied volatility of individual stocks.

Average three-month implied volatility among S&P 500 constituents stands at the 85th percentile of its historical range, compared with the 35th percentile for the VIX index.

HSBC said this difference indicates that volatility at the individual company level remains elevated relative to the broader market measure.

Corporate Earnings Season Could Provide Additional Market Support

HSBC expects third-quarter earnings announcements to contribute to equity market performance, based partly on recent patterns during corporate reporting periods.

Since 2025, the S&P 500 has recorded average gains of 4% during earnings reporting windows, compared with broadly unchanged performance outside those periods, according to the bank.

Pinder anticipates another reporting season in which companies exceed analysts' earnings expectations and raise their financial guidance.

HSBC noted that corporate guidance is improving at its fastest pace since 2021, providing support for its earnings outlook.

The bank also expects approximately $64 billion in customs refunds to contribute to corporate profit margins.
